deep.reconstruction:
This page has no text. It is the engraved plate (Comment. Nov. Acad. Petrop. Tom. VI, Tab. VI) that goes with Euler's E260, his attempt at a theory of friction of fluids flowing in pipes. The four figures show the pipe geometries the memoir treats.

Fig. 1: an element MNnm of a curved pipe ABCD of small bore. It is used to write the momentum (pressure) balance on a slice of fluid. In modern terms the balance includes a wall-friction force. Euler takes this force as acting along the wall and proportional to the pressure on the wall times the wetted perimeter, i.e. a Coulomb-type friction law carried over from solids. It is not the later viscous or empirical quadratic resistance.

Fig. 2: a vessel/reservoir (A, B, E) drains through a curved pipe ABNMDC. P is the foot of the horizontal from M on the vertical AS, so PM gives the depth or abscissa. MS is the normal to the curve at M, meeting the vertical in S, so MS is tied to the radius of curvature. Here the pressure on the wall comes not only from the hydrostatic and Bernoulli pressure but also from the centrifugal pressure of the fluid going round the bend. That curvature term enters the friction, because friction is taken proportional to pressure.

Fig. 3: a vessel AB-EF with a straight inclined pipe FD running down to the outlet CD at depth G. P and M mark a generic section. This is the simplest case: the pressure along the pipe follows a linear first-order ODE whose solution has exponential factors.

Fig. 4: a pipe made of successive straight segments BC, CD, DE at different inclinations, with levels F, G, H, I. The one-segment solution is applied segment by segment, giving composite exit velocities and fountain heights.

The preceding page (§120) applies the results to fountains. Friction reduces the effective head to roughly (4000 d/b)·q, and atmospheric pressure subtracts a further ~30 ft-equivalent in Euler's units. Euler concludes that jets should rise higher when the barometer is low.
errors: No mathematical content on this page to check. The plate is consistent with the geometric set-ups described in the text (normal MS at M, foot P on the vertical, piecewise-straight pipe).

ideas.what: Wall friction in pipe flow taken proportional to wall pressure (Coulomb-like law), including the centrifugal pressure in curved pipes (Fig. 2)
ideas.modern_name: One-dimensional pipe-flow momentum balance with a pressure-dependent friction law; curved-pipe (bend) losses
ideas.usually_credited_to: Pipe-resistance laws are usually credited to Chézy, Prony, Darcy and Weisbach (later 18th–19th c.); Euler's E260 is noted as an early, physically wrong pressure-proportional model
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 6 (1761); discussed in the Opera omnia II.13 editorial introduction (Truesdell)

ideas.what: Composition of the straight-pipe solution over a polygonal pipe (Fig. 4)
ideas.modern_name: Piecewise/segmentwise integration of a 1-D flow ODE

deep.surprise_reason: Plate page only; the figures merely illustrate configurations treated in the published text of E260, which is known and discussed in the literature.
transcription_corrections: Fig. 4 shows doubled labels for the two pipe walls at each node (A A, C C, D D, E E), not distinct points. Level marks F, G, H, I lie on the vertical axis.
Fig. 3: the second 'P' is the generic level of section MN; the upper 'P' is a separate mark on the vertical AE. The point at the bottom left is G.
